text_paragraph_2: Economic activity remained resilient in the first half of 2026, supported by services, agriculture and commodity exports. text_paragraph_3: Progress on reforms has strengthened confidence in a number of economies. Benin, Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana completed International Monetary Fund (IMF)-supported programmes in 2026, while Benin, Kenya, Ghana and Nigeria received sovereign rating upgrades during the year. In the near term, growth is expected to remain supported by agriculture, manufacturing, services and commodity production, although momentum is projected to soften as commodity windfalls fade.

When Education Becomes Too Expensive: Ghana Must Regulate Private Schools Better
text_paragraph_1: A child should not need a new set of textbooks every year when the same books can serve younger siblings. There is something fundamentally wrong when educating three children in the same family becomes unnecessarily expensive simply because they attend a private basic school.
text_paragraph_2: Consider this simple example. Alex is in Primary Six. His sister, Doreen is in Primary Four. Another sibling, Dora is in Primary Two. Alex finishes Primary Six. If his textbooks are still in good condition, why should those books not be passed down to his younger siblings when they eventually reach the same level?
text_paragraph_3: The mathematics is simple. One textbook bought today should ideally serve one child, then another, and perhaps another. The book becomes an educational asset of the family rather than a disposable commodity. Unfortunately, this principle appears increasingly difficult in parts of Ghana's private-school system. Some textbooks are designed as workbooks. Pupils are expected to write directly into them. Others are bundled with exercise books and supplementary materials. Some schools prescribe their own combinations of books and materials. Some schools change textbooks every academic year. When the academic year ends, the books cannot easily be passed on to younger siblings. For families with three or four children, the financial consequences can be considerable.

text_paragraph_1: East Africa remains Africa's fastest-growing region for a second consecutive year, but the African Development Bank now projects growth easing from 6.6% in 2025 to 5.9% in 2026, specifically citing rising energy and import costs linked to Middle East disruptions. That moderation isn't a story about weakening domestic demand. It's a story about a region whose growth model has become deeply dependent on imported Gulf fuel, and whose three largest economies are absorbing the exact same external shock from three genuinely different starting positions. Ethiopia keeps growing fastest and remains the most exposed to imported energy. Kenya is managing the tightest combination of inflation, debt and fiscal pressure. Tanzania is the one absorbing the shock with the most room to spare.
text_paragraph_2: NAIROBI — East Africa remains Africa's fastest-growing region for a second consecutive year, but the region's biggest advantage is now colliding directly with one of its biggest vulnerabilities. The African Development Bank's 2026 East Africa Economic Outlook, launched 28 July 2026 in Nairobi alongside a companion Kenya Country Focus Report, confirms regional growth accelerated sharply from 4.3% in 2024 to an estimated 6.6% in 2025, supported by resilient private consumption, expanding public and private investment, stronger agricultural production and a continuously growing services sector. The Bank now projects that growth easing to 5.9% in 2026, explicitly citing higher energy prices, geopolitical tensions and tighter global financial conditions linked to disruptions in the Middle East, before an anticipated rebound to 6.4% in 2027.
text_paragraph_3: The moderation the AfDB is projecting isn't primarily a domestic demand story. It's an external one. Higher energy and import costs, geopolitical tensions and supply chain disruptions are expected to weigh on activity across the region precisely because East Africa's growth model has become deeply dependent on sectors that require reliable, affordable energy to function at all. Manufacturing needs electricity and fuel. Agriculture needs fertiliser and transport. Tourism depends on aviation. Digital services depend on electricity and connectivity. Logistics depends on fuel. When energy prices rise, that shock doesn't stay contained to one sector, it spreads through almost every part of the economy simultaneously, which is precisely why one of Africa's fastest-growing regions can also be one of its more externally vulnerable ones at the same time.

text_paragraph_1: Small-scale farmers are facing mounting pressure from energy costs, climate extremes and conflict, with the strain reaching far beyond individual farms into food supplies, rural jobs and household incomes. Ten African countries have responded by increasing their contributions to the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), pledging nearly US$9 million and urging international partners to match their commitment. Their message places farmers and rural businesses at the centre of a larger economic question: how to build food systems that can withstand disruption and give people a dependable way to earn a living.
text_paragraph_2: Burundi, Chad, Ethiopia, Guinea, Kenya, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, Somalia, Sudan and Zimbabwe announced their pledges during the High-level Meetings of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly. The money will support IFAD's fourteenth replenishment, known as IFAD14, covering 2028–2030. Several countries have more than tripled their commitments, with the biggest increases approaching ten times their previous three-year contributions, signalling a stronger willingness to finance rural development and encourage greater support from other donors.
text_paragraph_3: Africa's largest generation of young people is entering the labour market, giving investment in rural economies an importance that extends beyond producing enough food. Stronger farms, agricultural businesses and market connections can create opportunities for young people, help communities cope with climate change and influence the continent's economic direction for decades. The pledges reflect a view shared by the participating countries that food security, economic opportunity and stability depend on giving rural communities the resources to grow.

title: Libya in Captivity... and Citizens Are Tired of Going Nowhere
text_paragraph_1: The Libyan crisis, with its intertwined local, regional, and international actors and interventions, remains deadlocked. There is nothing new to report and nothing from the past that has proved useful. The UN mission continues to search for a solution in the Libyan desert, while political fragmentation and division continue to strike different parts of the country. More alarming still is that time is passing quickly. Countries are building and developing, while Libya is not. Libya has chosen to remain stuck in 2011, with everything left in ruins.
text_paragraph_2: There is no doubt that negative external intervention is what has prolonged the Libyan crisis and transferred international disputes onto Libyan territory. After the state and its institutions were dismantled in 2011 under the pretext of protecting civilians, NATO left Libya for years at the mercy of the Muslim Brotherhood and its affiliated organizations. It then returned through a succession of international envoys, most of whom had failed in previous assignments. Why, then, are they sent in the first place to address a crisis as complex as Libya's? Thus, Libya became engulfed in a quagmire of terrorism and armed groups that infiltrated the country as a result of the chaos of the Arab Spring and the collapse of the state and its institutions, before the Libyan Army rose and regained control of most of the country.
text_paragraph_3: The Libyan crisis today reflects internal political divisions among different currents, some of which do not believe in the country's national geography. One such current is that of the isolated Grand Mufti, along with remnants of the Muslim Brotherhood, which uses the funds it obtained during the upheaval of the Arab Spring and its infiltration of centers of power and the Central Bank during the events of February 2011. It was able to rule for a period as a result of the political and presidential vacuum.

INTERVIEW/President Dan: Early elections mean four-five-six months of banners in the streets, ads, political squabbling
text_paragraph_1: AGERPRES special correspondent to New York, the U.S., Florin Stefan reports: Early elections mean four-five-six months of banners in the streets, TV commercials, quarrels among parties and I think that Romanians do not want this in any way, and the parties must do what the people who gave them the vote dictate, President Nicusor Dan said in an interview with AGERPRES on Wednesday in New York. The President also explained why he emphasised, in his first speech at the UN, the danger to democracy posed by manipulation through social media, saying that this phenomenon does not receive the necessary attention. Also, Dan said that the election of Dacian Ciolos at the head of the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF), one of the objectives pursued by Romania on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, could 'give a more pragmatic and more development-oriented and investment-oriented form to this organisation.' AGERPRES: Mr President, you began your first speech at the UN with a reference to the danger to democracy of manipulation through social media. Why did you choose this theme, which to many Romanians is associated with the reasons behind the cancellation of the 2024 presidential elections? Nicusor Dan: I chose this for a technical reason: I cut out what belongs to society from what belongs to the relations between societies, on the one hand, but, on the other hand, because, in my opinion, it is a very big danger to democracies. It is a danger that I have seen, at least in the interactions with European leaders, which are more frequent. I have seen it mentioned by each of them and it seems to me that we do not pay enough attention to this phenomenon. AGERPRES: Secondly, in your speech you asked for the support of the French-speaking countries for the candidacy of Mr Dacian Ciolos for the position of secretary general of the International Organisation of La Francophonie. What can Romania offer to African countries in addition to what Mr Ciolos' opponents in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mauritania or Rwanda have already offered? Nicușor Dan: Yes, first of all, a vision of what this organisation should be, because so far it has somehow been restricted to a cultural-academic area. Romania has contributed to that, starting from the tradition of students that we had in Romanian universities and some of whom are today in important positions in these countries. But the organisation did not focus on an economic development that would take advantage of these relationships of trust and culture that have developed between states. And I think that is what Dacian Ciolos, someone who knows how to work with banks, who knows how to work with medium and long-term programmes, can do: give a more pragmatic and more development-oriented and investment-oriented form to this organisation. AGERPRES: You have harshly criticised Russia in your three speeches, and you have also asked for the tightening of economic sanctions. Should we expect Romania's position to be firmer from now on in case of possible new violations of Romanian airspace? Nicusor Dan: No, our position has been constant. As far as airspace violations are concerned, we have tried to have, diplomatically, a proportionate response. However, in the speeches of last year, I focused more on pragmatic aspects: the sanctions regime, the concrete aid provided to Ukraine, the refugee situation, energy interconnections. But, in my opinion, it went without saying that we condemn the Russian aggression and support Ukraine. AGERPRES: If the government proposed by Siegfried Murean does not get Parliament's vote of confidence, do you consider triggering early elections? If not, what political solution do you envisage to avoid prolonging the crisis and a deterioration of citizens' trust in state institutions? Nicusor Dan: I want his government to pass. That is the reason why I made the appointment. I don't want to discuss too much about what will happen if it doesn't pass. In any case, early elections, to be clear to everyone, mean four-five-six months of banners in the streets, TV commercials, quarrels among parties, and I think Romanians don't want that in any way. So, in politics, in my opinion, you have to do pretty much what the people who voted for you dictate you to do. And that means the parties must, finally, find willingness to dialogue in order to come up with a solution. AGERPRES: Prime Minister-designate Siegfried Muresan has announced that he will suggest in the governing agenda a voluntary merger of small towns patterned on the model implemented by Moldova. Do you consider such an initiative appropriate? Nicusor Dan: (...) As you know, I was in Chisinau three or four weeks ago and I had a discussion with the prime minister. I saw this agenda and I think it is very good. Of course, the technical implementation mode must be discussed, but I think a merger of small towns, a voluntary one at the moment, is welcome. The Legacy of Morocco’s Gen Z Protests: Development as the New Political Language
text_paragraph_1: Moroccans head to the polls on September 23 in a parliamentary election that is meant to formally close the chapter opened during last year’s Gen Z 212 protests. The demonstrations, which erupted almost exactly a year ago, drew attention to the mismatch that exists between Morocco’s economic and geopolitical ambitions, and the stark reality of its lagging domestic development. Once the dust settled on the protests, some level of accountability was achieved , largely at the local level. But it was clear that the bigger reckoning would come at the level of national legislative politics. Party politics has since reflected that understanding: development has become a central theme for every major party in this election. Yet even as these parties put forward their proposals and hone their language around the issue, it remains unclear whether their measures would be able to overcome the structural constraints that have kept growth and public investments from producing broader social outcomes.
text_paragraph_2: The most visible casualty of the protests is already known. Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch announced in January that he would not seek re-election as head of his party and would not stand in the September elections. Under the party’s own rules, a leader cannot serve more than two terms, but the timing, coming after the Gen Z protests, signalled more than a routine handover. It hinted at an admission of political responsibility, if one with limited consequences, since his career as party leader was ending regardless.

Who gets to speak for Eritrea?
text_paragraph_1: E ritrea made its Miss World debut earlier this month, becoming one of the newest countries to join the competition since its founding in 1951. Miss Eritrea Snit Tewoldemedhin not only represented the country on this global platform for the first time—she won the People’s Choice Award . This achievement is a remarkable demonstration of Eritrean diaspora mobilization, but it’s not what stuck with me following the competition. In reality, the last beauty pageant I watched was probably Miss Congeniality , but as an Eritrean, it was impossible not to notice the paradox of Eritreans voting for the first time from a scattered diaspora, while those inside the country remain largely shut out of participation due to severe restrictions on internet access. It was equally impossible to overlook the irony of Miss Eritrea wearing a newspaper gown while representing a country with no freedom of the press.
text_paragraph_2: Following 30 years of struggle, Africa’s longest war for independence, Eritrea officially gained sovereignty from neighboring Ethiopia in 1993. Since then, the country has remained a one-party state with no formal elections since independence and no free press since 2001. While the world’s attention was on the September 11 attacks in the US, Eritrea shut down all independent newspapers and detained prominent dissenters, including journalists, politicians, and veteran liberation fighters. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) is presenting its 2026 International Press Freedom Award to the Eritrea 16 , marking “the 25th anniversary of the silencing of independent Eritrean media and the arrest of some of the world’s longest-detained journalists.”
text_paragraph_3: Though voices in the country are silenced, migration statistics speak louder than words. According to a 2025 report by the Migration Policy Institute , “one-third of the Eritrean-born population of about 6 million is estimated to live abroad,” citing indefinite mandatory military service, torture, and repressive humanitarian conditions as the cause for the growing exodus. Despite knowing the dangerous journey ahead, many Eritreans continue to flee across the border to neighboring Ethiopia or Sudan, and often onward toward horrific conditions in Libya, which has been the subject of many civil society protests in the European diaspora in recent weeks, including Justice for Eritreans’ September 12 protest in London .

MATI releases "El Niño: Voices of farmers," first-hand accounts from smallholder farmers in India and Zambia on El Niño and the 2026 harvest
text_paragraph_1: MATI today released El Niño: Voices of the Farmers, a field report available at el-nino.maticarbon.com, gathering first-hand accounts from smallholder farmers in India and Zambia on how the 2026 growing season unfolded under a strengthening El Niño. The report is published during Climate Week NYC and the high-level week of the United Nations General Assembly, where the effect of climate disruption on food systems is a central topic, and where the farmers most exposed to it are rarely heard directly. In September 2026, as forecasters upgraded the current El Niño to very strong, MATI asked farmers in both countries three questions: what changed in the weather this year, what it did to the farm and the family, and what they expect next year. The report carries each farmer's answers, in Hindi, English or Chitonga, with the recordings where they survive and a photograph taken at the interview. These are individual accounts rather than a survey, and they do not all agree with one another. MATI has published them as given.
text_paragraph_2: "Farmers are the first to see what a changing climate does to a harvest, and they are the last to be asked about it," said Shantanu Agarwal, CEO of MATI. "This El Niño has not yet reached its peak, and farmers in India are already describing a season that cost them money before it cost them yield. We are publishing their accounts so that the people meeting in New York this week can hear directly from the people whose livelihoods are on the line."
text_paragraph_3: El Niño is a periodic warming of the central and eastern Pacific that shifts rainfall patterns across much of the world. Its historical signature in the two regions covered by the report is well documented: a weaker and less reliable Indian summer monsoon, and dry conditions across southern Africa during the main rains on which Zambian maize depends. In its September 10, 2026 update, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center gave a greater than 90 percent chance of a very strong event through autumn and winter, and a 75 percent chance that October to December runs stronger than any El Niño on record back to 1950. Forecasters expect it to keep building through the end of 2026 and run into 2027. What the farmers in this report describe happened under an El Niño that was still strengthening. The season they are preparing for is the one ahead.

Who will watch power when journalists join it?
text_paragraph_1: Government ministries, corporations, universities, international organisations and development agencies increasingly employ former journalists as communication specialists, public relations practitioners and strategic advisers. The migration is understandable. Journalism is demanding, often poorly paid and increasingly insecure. Institutional communication frequently offers better salaries, stability and clearer career prospects. No reasonable person should condemn a journalist for seeking a better life.
text_paragraph_2: However, society must confront the consequence of this migration. Who watches power when those trained to watch it increasingly become part of its machinery? The issue is not that former journalists have somehow betrayed journalism by changing careers. It is that journalism loses more than an employee when an experienced reporter walks away. It loses institutional memory, investigative instincts, professional mentorship and the accumulated knowledge of how power operates. That loss matters. A young reporter can learn the mechanics of writing a story relatively quickly. Learning how to recognise when an official explanation does not quite add up takes years. It comes from knowing where to look, which questions to ask, which documents matter and when a seemingly minor inconsistency deserves a second investigation.

Zimbabwe launches School Health Policy
text_paragraph_1: 6 June 2018. Today Zimbabwe launched the School Health Policy as a strategic means to promote positive health determinants while preventing and mitigating health risks among learners. The policy, which was developed jointly by the Ministries of Health & Child Care and Primary and Secondary Education, has the vision of “A primary and secondary education system with an enabling environment for the provision of equitable, sustainable and quality health services for all learners.” The vision resonates well with the agenda for Universal Health Coverage. Through promoting health in schools, Zimbabwe can be sure that they are contributing to the aspiration of “leaving no one behind,” and an effective school health programme is one of the most cost effective investments a nation can make to simultaneously improve education and health. The launch was attended by the Ministers of Health and Child Care, and Primary and Secondary Education, other senior Government Officials, members of the UN family, development partners and civil society representatives.
text_paragraph_2: The Policy is seen as a bridge to engage the education sector in efforts to positively influence the educational, social and economic conditions that affect health. In addition, ensuring that a school-going-age population is healthy is key for the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). If health programming misses this age group it will be difficult to achieve the third SDG of Good health and well-being as well as the fourth goal on ensuring quality education, for without good health and provision of quality education it will not be possible to eradicate poverty (SDG 1). The policy, therefore, demonstrates that there should be strong interface between SDG3 and SDG4. The school Health Policy also presents an opportunity to address Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs) through Mass Drug Administration, Vitamin A and Iodine deficiencies; prevention of cancers such as cervical cancer through HPV vaccination among other public health interventions.
text_paragraph_3: In a speech read on his behalf by Mr Eddie Rowe, WFP Representative, the UN Resident Coordinator, Mr Bishow Parajuli said since the majority of adolescents and young people in Zimbabwe still spend the majority of their time in school, implementing a robust school health programme increases the reach of health promotion interventions in this age group. “HIV remains a significant public health concern in Zimbabwe especially among adolescents and youths, therefore, the School Health Program provides an opportunity for us to step up HIV prevention efforts among young people, and to promote adherence for those young people who are already on treatment,” said Mr Parajuli. He also said most social behaviours that influence alcohol and drug abuse are formed during the school going years, so the school has an important role to promote positive behaviours to curb these lifestyle ills. Mr Parajuli also urged the Ministries of Health and Education, development partners and stakeholders to work collectively to transform the strategies outlined in the policy document into practical programmes, plans and activities to ensure that all leaners benefit from the provisions of the policy.

Obasanjo’s Afro democracy
text_paragraph_1: With the steady erosion of democratic legitimacy in Africa and the strong wind of undemocratic change of governments that is blowing across the continent, from Burkina Faso to Mali, and from Niger to Gabon, the conversation on the future of democracy on the African continent continues. The latest intervention in this conversation has come from Olusegun Obasanjo, a former military head of state of Nigeria, who was later democratically elected its civilian President. An African statesman whose image looms large on the world stage as a champion of freedom, democratic good governance, anti-corruption and unity of the African people, Obasanjo’s experience as a major player in epoch-making events in Africa for more than half a century places him on a legitimate high ground to speak on the burning issues of democracy and good governance in Africa.
text_paragraph_2: Speaking at the high-level consultation on rethinking western liberal democracy in Africa, held at the Olusegun Obasanjo Presidential Library in Abeokuta, Ogun State, Obasanjo posited that western democracy as being practiced in Nigeria and other African countries should be re-examined or moderated. According to Nigeria’s former President, his position has become imperative because western liberal democracy has not delivered on good governance and progressive development for the continent. While describing western liberal democracy as not home-grown enough and never taking into account African history and multi-cultural peculiarities, hence, excluding the views of the majority, Obasanjo suggested its replacement with what he termed “Afro Democracy” as, according to him, “the essence of any system of government is the welfare and wellbeing of the people-all the people.”
text_paragraph_3: This latest intervention from Obasanjo has elicited mixed reactions, with many agreeing or disagreeing, depending on the prism through which his views are being viewed. But, as divided as opinions are on the opinion expressed by former President Obasanjo, all is not well with Nigeria’s democracy and many Nigerians share his frustrations about the state of affairs in Africa’s largest democracy. And such is the frustration that 24 years after unbroken democratic rule since the transition from military to civil democratic rule in 1999, the much anticipated dividends of democracy in the form of welfare and security for the Nigerian people remains elusive, leaving many Nigerians hopeless, helpless and questioning the relevance of democracy in the socio-economic development of their beloved Nigeria.

Obasanjo’s Afro democracy
text_paragraph_1: With the steady erosion of democratic legitimacy in Africa and the strong wind of undemocratic change of governments that is blowing across the continent, from Burkina Faso to Mali, and from Niger to Gabon, the conversation on the future of democracy on the African continent continues. The latest intervention in this conversation has come from Olusegun Obasanjo, a former military head of state of Nigeria, who was later democratically elected its civilian President. An African statesman whose image looms large on the world stage as a champion of freedom, democratic good governance, anti-corruption and unity of the African people, Obasanjo’s experience as a major player in epoch-making events in Africa for more than half a century places him on a legitimate high ground to speak on the burning issues of democracy and good governance in Africa.
text_paragraph_2: Speaking at the high-level consultation on rethinking western liberal democracy in Africa, held at the Olusegun Obasanjo Presidential Library in Abeokuta, Ogun State, Obasanjo posited that western democracy as being practiced in Nigeria and other African countries should be re-examined or moderated. According to Nigeria’s former President, his position has become imperative because western liberal democracy has not delivered on good governance and progressive development for the continent. While describing western liberal democracy as not home-grown enough and never taking into account African history and multi-cultural peculiarities, hence, excluding the views of the majority, Obasanjo suggested its replacement with what he termed “Afro Democracy” as, according to him, “the essence of any system of government is the welfare and wellbeing of the people-all the people.”
text_paragraph_3: This latest intervention from Obasanjo has elicited mixed reactions, with many agreeing or disagreeing, depending on the prism through which his views are being viewed. But, as divided as opinions are on the opinion expressed by former President Obasanjo, all is not well with Nigeria’s democracy and many Nigerians share his frustrations about the state of affairs in Africa’s largest democracy. And such is the frustration that 24 years after unbroken democratic rule since the transition from military to civil democratic rule in 1999, the much anticipated dividends of democracy in the form of welfare and security for the Nigerian people remains elusive, leaving many Nigerians hopeless, helpless and questioning the relevance of democracy in the socio-economic development of their beloved Nigeria.
